PCI.BIO: Dr. Hasina F. Huq is a Full Professor and the Department Chair  in the Department of Electrical & Computer Engineering at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). Dr. Huq's teaching and research interests include electronics, wide-bandgap semiconductor devices, biosensors, high temperature electronics and VLSI integrated circuits (IC) design. Her research work in these areas has been published widely in peer-reviewed journals as well as in conference proceedings (more than sixty research papers and book chapters). Dr. Huq was collaborating with Oak Ridge National Laboratories ORNL, Knoxville, TN for her research work. She worked with a team of researchers on wide band gap WBG semiconductors materials, their resistivity and processing issues. She served as a Principal investigator/co-principal investigator to many multi-year grants from the US Department of Defense (DoD), the National Science Foundation (NSF). Dr. Huq also received a grant from Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). She also served as a Panelist at the National Science Foundation (NSF) in the Division of Electrical, Communications and Cyber Systems. She is the recipient of the NanoHUB Education Scholarship (Purdue University), Network for Computational Nanotechnology award, Faculty Research Council (FRC) award, Summer Research Initiative award, Undergraduate Research Initiative (URI) award and Title V- HSI award. She served as a NSF ADVANCE STEM fellow at UTPA (2012-14). Dr. Huq is currently the director of the ‘Sputtering System Lab’ and one of the founder members of the “Microelectronics Research Laboratory, at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley. She is a member of the Institute for Electrical and Electronics Engineering (IEEE), Society of Women Engineers (SWE) and a member of the International Federation of University Women (IFUW).

CONGRANT.TITLE: DMREF: Harnessing Semiconductor Nanomaterials for High- Performance Biosensing: Emerging Materials and Strategies for Enhanced Sensitivity and Selectivity
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The rapid evolution of biosensing technology has catalyzed the development of novel semiconductive materials that possess exceptional electronic, optical, and biochemical properties, enabling precise and efficient detection of biomolecules and physiological signals. These materials, which range from two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors (e.g., graphene, MoS₂) to organic semiconductors and hybrid nanocomposites, are revolutionizing biosensor platforms through their sensitivity, selectivity, and adaptability. The success of these novel semiconductive materials in terms of these properties lies in their physical and chemical characteristics and the deeper understanding gained from computational physics. Advanced computational techniques have become indispensable tools for exploring the electronic structure, charge transport mechanisms, and biomolecular interactions of semiconductive materials at the atomic scale. These methods provide critical insights into the design and optimization of biosensing platforms, enabling the discovery of new materials tailored for specific sensing applications. The synergy between these advanced materials and computational physics has the potential to revolutionize healthcare and personalized medicine by offering non-invasive, accurate, and continuous monitoring of biomarkers, ensuring precision and efficient diagnosis of diseases.

CONGRANT.TITLE: 2021 MSEIP – Long-Range Improvement of Retention and Success Rates for UTRGV Hispanic Electrical and Computer Engineering Students
Rio Grande Valley Graduation Acceleration for Talented Engineering Students (RGV-GATES)
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The Rio Grande Valley Graduation Acceleration for Talented Engineering Students (RGV-GATES) program will provide scholarships to academically talented and financially needy engineering students to accelerate their graduation from the ABET-accredited Engineering at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) located in South Texas with a highly-concentrated Hispanic population.
From 2020-2025, the RGV-GATES program will fund, on average, 14 engineering scholarships every academic year to support academically promising students as they complete their undergraduate engineering degrees in a timely manner. Five cohorts of engineering students will be supported as they progress towards graduation, including one 2-year cohort, two 3-year cohorts, and two 4-year cohorts [Table 1]. Each cohort is considered complete once it reaches the end of its fourth year. The program will serve a total of 23 unduplicated students, including 11 recent high school graduates, and graduate 21 of them with bachelor’s degrees during the period of the program.
The mission of the program is to retain and graduate UTRGV engineering students within four years (or two years for students starting with an associate degree) of matriculation by providing an environment that supports them with college and engineering readiness, academic advising, peer and faculty mentoring, and assistance in the use of university resources.
Scholarships are to be awarded on the basis of both need and merit. The program aims to hold all participating students to high academic standards. Scholarship recipients must take 15 credit hours each semester and maintain a 3.0+ semester grade point average (GPA). The RGV-GATES program will enable a well-rounded student experience to promote learning and engagement beyond the classroom while maintaining rigorous academic expectations that compel students to maintain momentum toward timely degree completion. All scholarship recipients must apply for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) each spring to maintain their eligibility in the program.

CONGRANT.TITLE: MRI: Acquisition of a Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) for Advanced Materials Research and Education Programs at the Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
PROJECT SUMMARY

Overview:
The objective of the present MRI proposal is to acquire a state-of-the-art Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) that will support interdisciplinary research and education programs at UTRGV. The STEM combines the principles of transmission electron microscopy and scanning electron microscopy. The proposed instrument (Talos™ F200i) is flexible and compact 200 kV Field Emission Gun (FEG) STEM, designed for precise and quantitative characterization of nanomaterials and biological cells. It combines an outstanding quality in high-resolution STEM imaging with Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS). In addition, the instrument is equipped with tomographic capabilities via software for alignment of a tomographic series of images, and 3D reconstruction of the data.

Intellectual Merit:
The acquisition of the Talos™ F200i STEM instrument will enable a significant enhancement of basic research toolset across a wide range of materials, medical education and research programs including Chemistry, Physics, Medicine and Mechanical, Electrical and Manufacturing Engineering at UTRGV. Specifically, the proposed equipment will support projects to advance the development and characterization of different nanoparticles as lubricant additives, composite nanofibers, high entropy alloys (HEA) prepared by Selective Laser Melting technology, regenerative medicine, polymers, and nanomaterials for use in , patterned magnetic arrays, temperature controlled drug delivery systems, bioimaging, nanostructured energetic devices, semiconductors, high temperature superconductors, and radiation induced functional materials. The acquisition of the STEM will broaden the research scope for all participants, making it possible to address new scientific challenges in new transformative research directions.

Broader Impacts:
This proposal brings together a diverse group of faculty members and will significantly impact UTRGV transition towards an emerging research institution. In addition, most of the projects will be carried out by undergraduate and M.S. students. Specifically, the instrument will strengthen existing courses and several more will be developed as a result of this funding. Additionally, it will significantly support research and education programs operated at the DoD I-DREAM4D Consortium, which was recently funded by DoD on a $4 million grant and NSF PREM funded projects. It can also be integrated in the K12 outreach and education efforts organized by the colleges and the consortium at national scale. Results from the research projects supported by this instrument will be disseminated in peer journal articles and national/international conferences to stimulate further understanding and progress of the various research areas of the investigators discussed in this proposal. More importantly, this proposal will:1) Promote a hands-on, entrepreneurial, educational experience, and training of graduate and undergraduate students in advanced materials, nanomaterial design, biomaterials and characterization; 2) Enhance the research infrastructure at UTRGV; 3) Enhance the interdisciplinary research partnership between different departments at UTRGV to better compete for external funding; and 4) Increase the Hispanic Student retention rate at UTRGV

In summary, the Talos™ F200i instrument acquisition will strengthen the existing materials and medical research infrastructure at UTRGV and enhance the research and educational experiences of many students at UTRGV and South Texas region.

CONGRANT.TITLE: DoD-HBCUMI Equipment: Acquisition of an Advanced Materials’ Surface Characterization System for Science and Engineering Research and Education at South Texas
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The objective of this proposal is to acquire a state of the art surface characterization system including nano-indentation, micro-indentation, micro-scratch tester, and AFM that will support multidisciplinary research projects and education programs in areas of interest to DoD at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). The proposed system will include cutting-edge features needed to characterize a broad range of materials and provide the capability to investigate mechanical, tribological and other physical properties at nanostructured scales for materials that are too thin to be tested using conventional methods. In addition, UTRGV has in place a magnetron sputtering system (AJA International, A300) for research in physical vapor deposition (PVD). The acquisition of the proposed equipment will allow the surface characterization of the materials created by the sputtering system, which will immediately benefit research and educational projects in areas of interest to DoD. These projects include the following: (1) High temperature characterization of novel thermal barrier coatings created by PVD. Encompassing the development of novel PVD protective thermal barrier coatings TBC for gas turbine engines and the analytical methods to study their mechanical properties and adhesion to turbine blade materials at elevated temperatures. (2) Cost-effective CIGS thin films for novel solar power technology, encompassing the development of thin film solar cell like Copper Indium Gallium Di-Selenide (CIGS) with an optimized design considering the efficiency and cost effectiveness, to be used for space and satellite applications. Further, theoretical and numerical models will be developed, and the simulated result will be compared with experimental data. (3) Investigation of additive synthesis of intermetallic (IM) containing high entropy alloys (HEAs) directly from pure elemental powders using multiple metal additive manufacturing processes. Research in HEAs will open a nearly infinite space for novel engineering materials with trans-scale structures delivering superior properties required in extreme conditions normally expected in many defense systems. (4) Biointerfacing of functional nanofilaments for health/biothreat monitoring and life research. This project aims for the development of a novel functional system: Biohazard and Radiation Sensing (BRS). Integrated functional materials (IFM) will be grafted onto functional metal oxide with an immediate successive mesoporous micro layer surrounded by composite oxides. Advanced integrated materials systems with an innovative embedded BRS sensor system for real-time monitoring of biological and radiation hazards will be developed. (5) High energy density nanostructured composites with tailored particles size and shapes. The development of novel nanoenergetic materials, their design, synthesis and fabrication procedures are critical for national security and it was recognized as a significant addition to support advanced military formulations. The goal of this project is to explore the physics-based knowledge in energy release, shock waves and pressure discharge needed to enhance the performance and functionality of novel high density nanoenergetic composites with tailored particle shapes and size to reduce the mass and volume of munitions systems and components. The instrument will form a nucleus for a broad collaboration of scholars, resulting in further funding opportunities.  Additionally, the proposed equipment will facilitate efforts at UTRGV to reach out to traditionally underrepresented groups within science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields. The opportunity to participate in a state-of-the-art research projects motivates UTRGV students from a diverse background to pursue graduate school (M.S. or Ph.D. degrees). Furthermore, the acquisition of the proposed equipment will support development of physics, materials science, and engineering doctoral programs. Lastly, the proposed equipment will support the educational programs developed by the consortium for Innovation Driven Research/Education Ecosystem for Advanced Manufacturing for the Defense (I-DREAM4D) directed by Dr. J. Li at UTRGV.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Acquisition of an Electron Beam Lithography System for Enhancing Research and STEM Education in Nanophotonics and Biophysics
NSF MRI: Acquisition of a Surface Characterization Platform for Surface Engineering/Materials Research and Education Programs at the Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The objective of this Major Research Instrumentation (MRI) proposal is to acquire a cutting-edge mechanical surface characterization platform including nanoindentation, micro-indentation, micro-scratch tester, and AFM that will support multidisciplinary research and education programs at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV).
Nanoindentation is used to probe the mechanical properties of materials at the nano-size scale (approximately 10-7 to 10-9 meters). The system will include features needed to characterize a broad range of materials such as nanocrystalline alloys, polymer nanocomposite films, thin hard films, semiconductors, and conducting films from metallic nanoparticle dispersion precursors. The mechanical surface characterization platform will provide critical information about the behavior of materials for a variety of scientific and engineering challenges. It will create new opportunities to integrate research, education, training, and outreach. The capability to probe mechanical properties at nano-size scales is required for films that are too thin to test using conventional methods and for other materials whose properties are engineered by manipulating their structure at these small length scales. In addition, UTRGV has in place a magnetron sputtering system (AJA International, A300) for research in physical vapor deposition (PVD). The system is capable to create thin PVD ceramic films for different research areas. The acquisition of the mechanical surface characterization platform will immediately benefit research and educational projects in engineering, materials science, chemistry and physics at UTRGV.

NSF-MRI: Acquisition of a Sputtering System for Device and Material Research (SDMR) at Hispanic Gateway Institutions
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The objective of this research is to support ongoing multidisciplinary research and provide student training in semiconductor and thin film research through the acquisition of a Sputtering System for Device and Material Research at The University of Texas-Pan American and at The University of Texas at Brownsville. This approach is being taken to enrich the multidisciplinary research partnership and strengthen the collaboration between professors and students from the two institutions, attract new sources of research support, and elevate device and material education to a competitive level.

The intellectual merit is focused on finding solutions to multidisciplinary issues such as higher reliability, easier thermal management, and simpler manufacturing processes in semiconductor materials and devices. The project supports and promotes a hands-on, entrepreneurial, educational experience in micro-fabrication to enhance research infrastructure through characterization, improvement and development of thin films and electronics devices.

The broader impact includes academic enrichment in a historically underrepresented region of south Texas with a population of 1.5 million. The investigators will work to find out the key issues behind the low number of women entering the engineering discipline and to explain the necessity of having more women involved in this technology-related field. The acquisition will also help to prepare qualified and skilled graduate and undergraduate students and lays the foundation for strong integrated research and education initiatives centered on devices and materials at Minority Serving Institutions.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Multidirectional Pin-on-Disk Testing Device to Evaluate the Cross-shear Effect on the Wear of Biocompatible Materials

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: UTRGV

INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Instruments
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: One of the main causes of hip prostheses failure is the premature wear of their components. Multi-directional motion or “cross-shear” motion has been identified as one of the most significant factors affecting the wear rate of UHMWPE in total hip joint replacement prostheses. To better evaluate the effect of this cross-shear motion on the tribological behavior of different biomaterials, a new wear testing device has been designed and developed. This new instrument is capable to reproduce the “cross-shear” effect with bidirectional motion on bearing materials and to determine coefficient of friction (COF) between surfaces during testing. To validate the functionality of this new testing platform, alumina balls were articulated against Ti-6Al-4V ELI alloy disks in Ringer’s solution. Four different articulation patterns, all with identical path lengths per cycle, were tested. Gravimetric weight loss was converted to volumetric wear data in order to determine the effects of motion patterns on the wear. Worn surfaces were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy. This scientific approach to quantifying the tribological effects of cross-shear provides fundamental data that are crucial in evaluating potential biomaterials for use in knee and hip joint replacements.

PRESENT.TITLE: Comparison of Two Synthesis Methods to Deposit Silicon Nitride (Si3N4) thin films.
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Silicon nitride thin film is a well-known kind of material in semiconductor industries. These films are used in important applications such as protective layers; insulators for optical devices, etc. It is also an important material in microelectronics due to its high resistivity, higher dielectric constant compared to silicon dioxide, mechanical strength, and chemical inertness. It is used as a gate insulator in thin film transistors that are in flat panel displays. In this work we have fabricated Silicon Nitride (Si3N4) thin films using RF magnetron sputtering method using Si3N4 Target. P-doped, N-doped Si wafers, sapphire wafers and glass plates are used as substrate material. We will also fabricate Silicon nitride thin films with Si target and N2 as process gas. It will be cost effective because Si targets are cheaper than Si3N4 targets. To compare the sputtered grown samples from both recipes, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) will be employed. Both high and low temperatures will be used for depositions so that we can find out the optimum conditions for silicon nitride deposition with highest purity possible. Silicon nitride films are mainly prepared by chemical vapor deposition (CVD) and plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD).
